title: EcoFlow vs Jackery: EcoFlow for Home Backup, Jackery to Carry
metaDescription: EcoFlow wins for home backup with add-on batteries and 1,800 W on the Delta 3 Plus; Jackery's Explorer 1000 v2 packs 1,070 Wh into about 24 lb for camping.
intro:
The two biggest names in portable power compared size class by size class, from 300 Wh camping boxes to 240 V home systems, with a straight verdict for camping, outages and whole-home backup.

EcoFlow sells a platform you can grow; Jackery sells an appliance you can carry. At every size class that one difference decides more than any spec sheet, and once you know which you need, the choice takes about a minute.

sections.heading: The Short Answer: Platform vs. Appliance
sections.body:
If you have searched for a "Jackery solar generator" or an "EcoFlow power station," you have probably noticed that the two brands chase each other model for model. Each sells a small camping box around 300 Wh, a 1 kWh all-rounder, a 2 kWh step-up and a big wheeled unit aimed at home backup. Each uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells on its current models, charges from the wall in about an hour at the 1 kWh size, and bundles its own folding solar panels. On the surface, it looks like a coin toss.

It is not quite one. The two companies have made different bets, and those bets show up in the details that decide what living with the box is like. EcoFlow builds platforms: most of its stations accept add-on batteries, talk to a smart home panel, and expose a lot of settings through an app. Jackery builds appliances: its popular Explorer v2 models are lighter for their capacity, simpler to run, and fixed in size. Neither approach is better in the abstract. Which one suits you depends on whether you expect your needs to grow, how far you plan to carry the thing, and how much you want to fiddle with it.

This comparison works through the lineups one size class at a time, then looks at the things spec sheets bury: ecosystems, charging behavior, weight per watt-hour, apps and warranty. Everything here is drawn from the manufacturers' published specifications rather than hands-on testing, and model details change often, so confirm the figures on the listing you buy from. If you are still deciding how big a battery you need at all, start with our [portable power station buying guide](/best-portable-power-station/) and come back here once you know your size class.

THE SHORT ANSWER

EcoFlow if you want room to grow. Jackery if you want the lightest, simplest box.

EcoFlow wins on add-on batteries, 240 V home backup, a smart panel and the most output per size class. Jackery wins on weight and simplicity at a given capacity. At 1 kWh, the Delta 3 Plus wins on output and expandability; the Explorer 1000 v2 wins on weight. For home backup, the Delta Pro 3 is the more complete system.

The table below shows how the head-to-head shakes out across the categories most buyers care about. A "win" means the brand's current lineup is stronger on that point for most people, not that the other brand is weak. Notice that the wins split fairly evenly; the useful question is which of these rows actually matters for the way you will use the station, and the rest of this guide is organized to help you answer exactly that.

| Category | EcoFlow | Jackery | Edge |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Output at 1 kWh | 1,800 W (Delta 3 Plus) | 1,500 W, 3,000 W surge (Explorer 1000 v2) | EcoFlow |
| Weight at 1 kWh | ~28 lb | ~24 lb | Jackery |
| Expandability | Most models accept add-on batteries | Popular v2 models are fixed size | EcoFlow |
| 2 kWh in one box | Reached by adding a battery | Explorer 2000 v2, ~40 lb | Jackery |
| Whole-home backup | Delta Pro 3, 4,096 Wh, 120/240 V | Larger Explorer Plus systems | EcoFlow |
| Ease of use | Many settings, app-centric | Fewer settings, simpler | Jackery |
| Battery chemistry | LFP | LFP | Tie |
| Warranty (current models) | Roughly five years | Roughly five years | Tie |

Throughout this guide, runtime estimates use one simple rule: runtime in hours is roughly the capacity in watt-hours times 0.85, divided by the average load in watts. The 0.85 factor accounts for inverter losses and the small reserve every station holds back. It is not exact for every model, but it is close enough to compare the two brands fairly, and it is the same arithmetic you should run on your own load list before you buy anything.

sections.heading: The Two Brands and the Four Models Worth Comparing
sections.body:
Jackery popularized the portable power station in the U.S. and still owns the phrase "Jackery solar generator" in a lot of people's heads. Its Explorer line has always prioritized portability and simplicity: a handle on top, a clear display, a sensible set of outlets, and few decisions to make. The current v2 generation moved the popular sizes to LFP cells, added much faster wall charging and introduced app control, but the products are still built around the idea that a power station should be a self-contained appliance you buy at the size you need.

EcoFlow came to market later and made charging speed its calling card, then built outward into a full energy ecosystem. Its River line covers small portable units, the Delta line covers the 1 kWh to 4 kWh range, and the Delta Pro models are designed to sit at the center of a home backup system with extra batteries, smart panels, alternator chargers and rigid solar panels. The products are typically a little heavier and more feature-dense, with more configuration options exposed through the EcoFlow app.

Both brands sell the same models under different bundle names. An "EcoFlow solar generator" or "Jackery solar generator" is simply one of these stations sold with the brand's folding panels and cables; there is no separate machine inside. Our [solar generator guide](/best-solar-generator/) covers when a bundle is good value and when buying the panels separately works out cheaper.

Out of each lineup, two models matter most for this comparison: the 1 kWh all-rounder that most people should look at first, and the bigger unit each brand would point you to for longer outages. The four are summarized below from the manufacturers' published specifications, and each gets a fuller treatment in the size-class sections that follow.

| Model | Role | Capacity | AC output | Weight |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus | Best EcoFlow overall | 1,024 Wh LFP, expandable | 1,800 W | ~28 lb |
| Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 | Best Jackery overall | 1,070 Wh LFP | 1,500 W (3,000 W surge) | ~24 lb |
| EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 | Best EcoFlow for home backup | 4,096 Wh LFP, expandable | 4,000 W, 120/240 V | ~114 lb |
| Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 | Best Jackery for longer outages | 2,042 Wh LFP | 2,200 W | ~40 lb |

The pattern is visible even in four rows. The EcoFlow models carry the word "expandable" and the higher output figures; the Jackery models carry the lower weights. That trade repeats at every size, so if you already know which side of it you care about, you can probably skip to the verdict table at the end. If you do not, the size-class sections below show where the trade bites and where it does not.

sections.heading: Small Class: About 300 Wh
sections.body:
At the bottom of each lineup sit the units most people buy for camping, tailgates, a go-bag or a desk UPS. EcoFlow's entry is the River 3 Plus; Jackery's most direct counterpart is the Explorer 300 Plus. Both are small enough to carry in one hand and both use LFP cells, so on paper they look like twins until you get to the inverter line.

|  | EcoFlow River 3 Plus | Jackery Explorer 300 Plus |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Capacity | 286 Wh LFP | 288 Wh LFP |
| AC output | 600 W | 300 W |
| Weight | ~10 lb | Comparable small-carry size |
| Expandable | Yes, with a snap-on extra battery | No |
| Usable AC energy (Wh x 0.85) | ~243 Wh | ~245 Wh |
| Strongest at | Running small appliances, UPS duty | Charging phones, laptops and cameras |

Capacity is a wash; the two batteries differ by two watt-hours. The meaningful gap is the inverter. EcoFlow rates the River 3 Plus at 600 W, which covers a small blender, a projector, a mini fridge, a soldering station or a CPAP with room to spare. Jackery lists the Explorer 300 Plus at 300 W, which is plenty for laptops, a camera charger, string lights, a fan and a 12 V cooler, but not for anything with a heating element or a meaningful motor.

The River also has an expansion path: EcoFlow's optional extra battery for the River 3 series roughly triples its capacity, turning a day-trip box into a weekend box without buying a second station. The Jackery stays at 288 Wh for its whole life. For a unit that will mostly charge devices that is no hardship, but it does mean the only upgrade is a second purchase.

### Worked Example: Two Nights at a Campsite

A 12 V compressor cooler averaging 45 W for 48 hours uses about 2,160 Wh, which is already far beyond either unit on its own and surprises a lot of first-time buyers. Drop the cooler to ice and the budget looks very different: LED lights at 10 W for 10 hours (100 Wh), four phone charges (80 Wh) and a camera battery or two (30 Wh) total about 210 Wh, comfortably inside either unit's roughly 245 Wh of usable energy, even before a small panel tops it up. For a trip that includes a powered cooler, either add 100 to 200 W of solar or step up to the 1 kWh class. Our [camping power station guide](/best-portable-power-station-for-camping/) works through full trip budgets like this one.

Small-class winner: EcoFlow, on the strength of double the output and the expansion option. If your list is strictly phones, laptops and lights, the Jackery is just as capable, and for that job you may not need a power station at all; our roundup of [portable chargers for power outages](/best-portable-chargers-for-power-outages/) covers lighter, cheaper ways to keep devices alive.

sections.heading: 1 kWh Class: Delta 3 Plus vs. Explorer 1000 v2
sections.body:
This is the class where most buyers end up and where the brands are closest. Both units store about a kilowatt-hour in LFP cells, both charge from the wall in roughly an hour, both work as an uninterruptible supply for a home office, and both lift into a car trunk. The differences are output, weight and what happens when you outgrow them.

|  | EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus | Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Capacity | 1,024 Wh LFP | 1,070 Wh LFP |
| Usable AC energy | ~870 Wh | ~910 Wh |
| Continuous output | 1,800 W | 1,500 W |
| Surge | Higher than continuous for motor starts | 3,000 W |
| Weight | ~28 lb | ~24 lb |
| Wh per pound | ~37 | ~45 |
| Expandable | Yes | No |
| Wall charge | About an hour | About an hour in the app's fast mode |

The Delta 3 Plus is EcoFlow's answer for the household that wants one box to cover outages, camping and a bit of solar. Its 1,024 Wh battery yields roughly 870 Wh of usable AC energy by the runtime rule, enough to keep a modern refrigerator running for most of a day or a router and CPAP going for several nights. The other reason to buy it is what happens later: clip on an EcoFlow extra battery and you have a roughly 2 kWh system without replacing anything. The price of that flexibility is about four extra pounds and an interface that rewards people who like to tune charge limits and modes in the app.

Jackery's Explorer 1000 v2 is the most direct rival and, for a lot of buyers, the more pleasant one to own. It stores a little more energy, 1,070 Wh or about 910 Wh usable, in a lighter case. That gap matters more than it sounds when you are carrying the box from a car to a campsite or up from a basement during an outage. Where it gives ground is ceiling: continuous output stops at 1,500 W, there is no add-on battery, and the fastest wall charging has to be switched on in the app. If you are confident 1 kWh is your size, those limits rarely bite, and the simplicity is a feature.

### What the 300 W Gap Means

A 1,500 W ceiling and an 1,800 W ceiling sound close, but a lot of household appliances live between them. Many full-size microwaves draw 1,200 to 1,500 W from the wall, kettles and toasters often draw 1,500 to 1,800 W, and a hair dryer on high is commonly around 1,800 W. On the Jackery, those loads either trip the inverter or leave no room for the fridge to cycle on at the same moment. On the EcoFlow, most of them fit, as long as nothing else large is running. If your outage plan includes making coffee or heating food in a microwave, that is a practical reason to lean EcoFlow. For motor loads the comparison is closer: a refrigerator compressor may pull 600 to 1,200 W for a moment at start-up, and the Jackery's 3,000 W surge rating swallows that comfortably.

### Runtime Side by Side

| Average load | Delta 3 Plus (~870 Wh) | Explorer 1000 v2 (~910 Wh) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Router + modem (20 W) | ~43 hrs | ~45 hrs |
| CPAP without heated humidifier (40 W) | ~22 hrs | ~23 hrs |
| Refrigerator, 1.5 kWh/day (avg. ~63 W) | ~14 hrs | ~14 hrs |
| Fridge + router + lights (~110 W avg.) | ~8 hrs | ~8 hrs |
| Box fan on medium (50 W) | ~17 hrs | ~18 hrs |

Worked example, a summer evening outage: the power drops at 6 p.m. You want the fridge (averaging about 63 W on a 1.5 kWh-per-day model), the router (20 W), two LED lamps (20 W) and a box fan (50 W) until the grid returns. That is roughly 153 W on average. The Delta 3 Plus lasts about 5.7 hours and the Explorer 1000 v2 about 5.9 hours, so both get you to around midnight. Turn the fan off when you go to bed and both stretch past breakfast. The decision between them is not runtime; it is whether you want the extra 300 W of output and the option to add a battery, or the lighter case.

1 kWh winner: EcoFlow for most households, Jackery for carriers. If the box will mostly live in the house for outages, the Delta 3 Plus's output and expansion path win. If it will spend most of its life in a car, an RV or a campsite, the Explorer 1000 v2's lighter case and simpler controls make it the nicer companion.

sections.heading: 2 kWh Class: Explorer 2000 v2 vs. an Expanded Delta
sections.body:
At 2 kWh the brands take genuinely different routes. Jackery sells a single 2 kWh box. EcoFlow's most natural way to the same capacity is a Delta 3 Plus with one of its extra batteries attached, which roughly doubles storage. That gives you a fair way to compare the two philosophies directly, because the usable energy ends up almost identical.

|  | Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 | EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus + extra battery |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Total capacity | 2,042 Wh LFP | About 2,048 Wh LFP |
| Usable AC energy | ~1,740 Wh | ~1,740 Wh |
| Continuous output | 2,200 W | 1,800 W (set by the main unit) |
| Form | One box, ~40 lb | Two boxes plus a cable |
| Split it up? | No | Yes: take the 1 kWh unit camping, leave the battery home |
| Grow further? | No | Yes, with a second extra battery |

The Explorer 2000 v2 is where Jackery's lightweight approach pays off most. Jackery lists 2,042 Wh, roughly 1,740 Wh usable, in a single case of about 40 pounds, which works out to around 51 Wh per pound. Getting to the same capacity with EcoFlow means two boxes, a connecting cable and more total weight. For RV owners and anyone who wants to carry a full day of refrigerator power to the car in one trip, that is a real advantage, and it is the simpler unit to hand to someone else in an emergency.

Its 2,200 W inverter runs a microwave, a coffee maker or a sump pump start, and the capacity covers a fridge for about a day, or a fridge plus CPAP, router and lights through a typical overnight outage. That is 400 W more continuous output than the EcoFlow stack, because the stack is limited by the Delta 3 Plus's own inverter. The limits are the same as the 1000 v2: 120 V only and no add-on batteries. If you think you will someday want 240 V or a smart panel, buy into an expandable platform instead.

The EcoFlow stack wins on flexibility. Buy the Delta 3 Plus this year, add the battery when you find 1 kWh too tight, and you can still unclip the main unit and take a lighter box camping. If a few years from now you want even more, a second extra battery pushes the system further. You are paying for that modularity with lower peak output and more pieces to keep track of.

### Worked Example: An Overnight Winter Outage with CPAP

The furnace is gas but its blower is plugged in, so it needs about 400 W while running and perhaps 30% of the time on a cold night, roughly 120 W on average. Add the fridge (63 W average), CPAP (40 W) and router (20 W) and the average load is about 243 W. Either 2 kWh setup lasts about 7 hours by the runtime rule, long enough to get through a night if you let the fridge rest for a few hours. Plugging a furnace blower into a station requires a properly installed inlet or a transfer switch rather than an improvised cord, which we cover in our [home backup power station guide](/best-portable-power-station-for-home-backup/).

2 kWh winner: Jackery, for anyone who wants this capacity in one easily moved box. Choose the EcoFlow stack if you value starting smaller and growing, or splitting the system between home and trips.

sections.heading: Whole-Home Class: Delta Pro 3 and Jackery's Big Systems
sections.body:
Above 3 kWh, portable power stations stop being carry-around boxes and become wheeled home batteries. This is where EcoFlow has its strongest product. EcoFlow rates the Delta Pro 3 at 4,096 Wh of LFP storage, about 3,480 Wh usable, behind a 4,000 W inverter that can deliver both 120 V and 240 V. That 240 V capability is what lets it run many deep well pumps and other split-phase loads that no 1 kWh or 2 kWh unit from either brand can touch.

Add EcoFlow's extra batteries and the capacity scales into the tens of kilowatt-hours; add its smart home panel or a transfer switch and the station powers selected house circuits directly. The trade-offs are real: at about 114 pounds it moves on wheels, not by hand, the panel connection needs a licensed electrician, and the full setup with panels and switchgear is a large outlay. But it is the most complete battery backup system either brand sells.

Jackery's answer is its larger Explorer Plus systems, led by a roughly 5 kWh flagship designed around expansion batteries, 240 V output and a transfer switch for home use. Model names, capacities and bundles in this tier change frequently, so rather than quote figures we cannot pin down for every current variant, the table compares what each platform offers.

|  | EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 | Jackery's large Explorer Plus systems |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Base capacity | 4,096 Wh LFP | Roughly 5 kWh class on the flagship; check the listing |
| Output | 4,000 W, 120/240 V | 240 V-capable on the flagship |
| Weight | ~114 lb, wheeled | Wheeled, similar heavy class |
| Expansion | Add-on batteries into the tens of kWh | Add-on batteries supported |
| Home integration | Smart home panel or transfer switch | Jackery transfer switch or standard switchgear |
| Maturity of ecosystem | Broad, several generations of home products | Newer and narrower |

### Worked Example: A Two-Day Storm Outage

A household wants to keep a fridge (1.5 kWh/day), a chest freezer (about 1 kWh/day), the furnace blower (about 3 kWh/day in cold weather), lights and internet (about 0.8 kWh/day) and a well pump that uses perhaps 1 kWh/day. That is roughly 7.3 kWh a day. The Delta Pro 3 on its own provides about 3,480 Wh usable, just under half a day at that rate. One extra battery roughly doubles it, and 1,600 W of panels in a sunny spell can put back several kilowatt-hours a day at a realistic 60 to 75% of rating over four to five peak sun hours. That is how battery systems reach multi-day coverage: storage to get through the night, solar to refill during the day, and some discipline about what stays on.

Both brands can be configured to do this job. EcoFlow's advantage is that the Delta Pro 3 platform has been through more generations of home-backup hardware and offers more ways to integrate with a house. Before you commit to either, compare the full installed cost of station, extra batteries, panel hardware and electrician with a standby generator using our [Generac generator cost guide](/generac-generator-cost/), and with a fuel-burning unit using our [home generator guide](/best-home-generator-for-power-outages/). For long outages with heavy loads, gas or propane is often still the cheaper answer.

Whole-home winner: EcoFlow. The Delta Pro 3 is the more complete, more proven home system. Jackery's large units are worth a look if you prefer the brand or find a strong bundle, but compare the ecosystem carefully before you commit several thousand dollars to it.

sections.heading: Ecosystems, Charging Speed and Solar
sections.body:
An ecosystem is everything you can add to the station after you buy it. For a camping box that hardly matters; for a home-backup purchase it is most of the decision. The table summarizes what each brand offers today, and it explains a lot of the size-class verdicts above.

| Accessory | EcoFlow | Jackery |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Add-on batteries | Available across River, Delta and Delta Pro lines | Available for large Explorer Plus models; not for the popular v2 sizes |
| Folding solar panels | Wide range of portable panels | SolarSaga range, widely bundled |
| Rigid panels | Offered for permanent arrays | Limited |
| Smart home panel | Yes, for Delta Pro class | Transfer switch for large models |
| Vehicle charging | Car socket input; dedicated alternator charger offered | Car socket input |
| Third-party panels | Usually work within voltage and current limits | Usually work within voltage and current limits |

EcoFlow's ecosystem is broader and older. If you want to start with a 1 kWh station and gradually build toward a solar-backed home system, EcoFlow has more pieces that fit together. Jackery's ecosystem is narrower but well integrated where it exists: the SolarSaga panels pair cleanly with every Explorer, and its large-model expansion batteries and transfer switch cover the home-backup basics. One caution applies to both: an ecosystem is a lock-in. Add-on batteries from one brand do not fit the other, and smart panels are brand-specific. Solar panels are the exception, which makes them the safest accessory to buy first.

EcoFlow made very fast wall charging its signature early on, and Jackery has largely caught up in the v2 generation. At the 1 kWh size, both brands now quote roughly an hour from empty to full on a household outlet: the Jackery in a fast or "emergency" mode enabled through its app, the EcoFlow by default. The practical difference is small, but a Jackery straight out of the box may charge more slowly until you change the setting. Fast charging matters in a rolling outage, where the grid flickers back for an hour or two between failures; a station that refills in an hour is ready for the next drop, and one that takes four or five hours is not.

### Solar Refill Times

Solar charging is limited by the panels far more than by the station. A portable panel typically delivers about 60 to 75% of its rated wattage in good midday sun, and a clear day provides the equivalent of four to five peak sun hours. That gives a simple estimate for any of these units, whichever logo is on the case.

| Panels connected | Realistic daily harvest | ~300 Wh station | ~1 kWh station | ~2 kWh station |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 100 W | ~240-375 Wh | About a full refill | About a third | About a sixth |
| 200 W | ~480-750 Wh | Full, with surplus | Roughly half to three-quarters | About a third |
| 400 W | ~960-1,500 Wh | Full, with surplus | Full on a good day | Half to three-quarters |
| 800 W | ~1,900-3,000 Wh | n/a | Full, with surplus | Full on a good day |

Each station has a maximum solar input wattage and voltage range. The larger EcoFlow units generally accept more solar wattage than their Jackery counterparts at the same size class, which matters if you plan a permanent array; for a couple of folding panels at a campsite, either brand's input limit is rarely the bottleneck. Check the specific figures on the model you buy before wiring panels in series, because cold, bright mornings push open-circuit voltage up.

sections.heading: Weight per Watt-Hour, Apps and Warranty
sections.body:
Weight per watt-hour is the best single number for comparing how portable two power stations really are. It tells you how much energy you get for every pound you lift. Using the published capacities and approximate weights, including two rival brands for context:

| Model | Capacity | Weight | Wh per pound |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 | 2,042 Wh | ~40 lb | ~51 |
| Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 | 1,070 Wh | ~24 lb | ~45 |
| Bluetti Elite 100 V2 | 1,024 Wh | ~25 lb | ~41 |
| EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus | 1,024 Wh | ~28 lb | ~37 |
| EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 | 4,096 Wh | ~114 lb | ~36 |
| Anker SOLIX C300X | 288 Wh | ~9 lb | ~32 |
| Anker SOLIX F3800 | 3,840 Wh | ~132 lb | ~29 |
| EcoFlow River 3 Plus | 286 Wh | ~10 lb | ~29 |

Jackery sits at the top of the table, and that is not an accident: light weight has been the brand's priority from the start. EcoFlow's units carry more weight per watt-hour, partly because they pack higher-output inverters, more ports and expansion connectors into each case. Small units always score worse on this measure because the case, inverter and outlets weigh roughly the same whatever the battery size. For a unit that lives in a utility closet and gets wheeled out twice a year, it barely matters. For a unit you carry from a car to a campsite every other weekend, four pounds at 1 kWh and a whole second box at 2 kWh are differences you feel every trip.

### Apps

Both brands now offer phone apps that connect over Wi-Fi or Bluetooth and show state of charge, input and output watts, and estimated runtime. EcoFlow's app is the deeper of the two: it exposes charge and discharge limits, charging speed, AC and DC output toggles, standby timers and, on the larger units, home-panel circuit control and energy scheduling. That depth is great for people who like to tune a system and slightly overwhelming for those who do not. Jackery's app is simpler, and the stations are designed to be used without it; the main reason to install it is to switch on fast charging and adjust a few battery-protection settings. If you are buying for a parent who will never open an app, that counts in Jackery's favor.

One tip for either brand: set the charge limits and update the firmware once, at home, before you need the station. Outages are a bad time to discover that a feature lives behind an app login, and a cellular network under storm load is a bad time to download a firmware update.

### Warranty, Support and Longevity

Both brands offer roughly five years of warranty coverage on their current LFP models, the clearest signal that each trusts its cells and inverters for the long haul. Terms vary by model, by retailer and by whether you register the product, so read the warranty page for the specific unit and keep proof of purchase. Both companies are large and widely stocked in the U.S., with replacement cables, chargers and accessories easy to find. Both use LFP chemistry rated for thousands of cycles, so either should outlast the warranty with sensible storage: keep it at 50 to 80% charge, top it up every few months, and avoid charging below freezing. If the station lives in a damp basement next to a basement dehumidifier, keep it off the floor and away from condensation.

sections.heading: The Alternatives and the Verdict by Use Case
sections.body:
EcoFlow and Jackery are not the only serious choices, and comparing them only to each other can hide a better deal. Bluetti often competes on price. Bluetti rates the Elite 100 V2 at 1,024 Wh of LFP storage and 1,800 W of output, matching the Delta 3 Plus on paper in a roughly 25-pound case that is lighter than the EcoFlow. Its ecosystem and app are less developed, but if it is discounted below both big names, it is a strong 1 kWh buy.

Anker SOLIX competes at both ends. The SOLIX C300X is a 288 Wh LFP unit with a 300 W inverter at about 9 pounds, a natural rival to the small Jackery for charging duty. At the top, Anker lists the SOLIX F3800 with 3,840 Wh of LFP storage and a 6,000 W, 120/240 V inverter, more output than the Delta Pro 3, at about 132 pounds. If your critical load is a big 240 V well pump or emergency EV charging, the F3800 deserves a place on the shortlist alongside the EcoFlow. Our main [best portable power stations](/best-portable-power-station/) roundup ranks all four brands together if you want to see them side by side.

| If you mainly want... | Pick | Why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Day trips, tailgates, a desk UPS | EcoFlow River 3 Plus | 600 W output and an expansion option |
| Phones and laptops only | Jackery Explorer 300 Plus or a power bank | Same capacity; output is not the constraint |
| Camping and RV weekends at 1 kWh | Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 | Lighter, simpler, more Wh |
| Home outages at 1 kWh | EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus | 1,800 W and room to grow |
| 2 kWh in one box | Jackery Explorer 2000 v2 | Best capacity per pound, 2,200 W |
| Start small, grow later | EcoFlow Delta 3 Plus | Add batteries as needs grow |
| Whole-home, 240 V, solar | EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 | Most complete home ecosystem |
| Heaviest 240 V loads | Anker SOLIX F3800 (alternative) | 6,000 W output |

Choose EcoFlow if the station will spend most of its life at home, you want the most output in each size class, you like the idea of adding batteries or a smart panel later, and you do not mind an app with a lot of settings. EcoFlow wins the small class, the at-home 1 kWh decision and the whole-home class.

Choose Jackery if you will carry the station often, you know the size you need, and you want an appliance that works without fuss. Jackery wins on portability at every size and offers the best single-box 2 kWh unit of the two.

If you are torn at 1 kWh, ask one question: will you ever want 2 kWh? If the answer is "maybe," buy the Delta 3 Plus and add a battery later. If the answer is "no," the Explorer 1000 v2 is lighter and just as capable for the jobs you have in mind. And whichever you choose, the sizing arithmetic matters more than the logo: the right size from either brand beats the wrong size from the "better" one.

mistakes.title: Choosing by brand before choosing by size
mistakes.body: The capacity and output decision matters far more than the logo. A 1 kWh EcoFlow and a 1 kWh Jackery run a fridge for nearly the same time, while either one is wrong if your load list needs 2 kWh. Add up your average watts and hours first, then pick the brand that fits that size class.

mistakes.title: Assuming 1,500 W runs every kitchen appliance
mistakes.body: Kettles, toasters and hair dryers often draw 1,500 to 1,800 W, which puts them right at or past the Explorer 1000 v2's continuous limit. If coffee or microwave meals are part of your outage plan, check the wattage label on each appliance before deciding a 1,500 W inverter is enough.

mistakes.title: Buying a fixed-size unit when needs may grow
mistakes.body: Jackery's popular v2 models cannot take an add-on battery, so outgrowing one means selling it or buying a second unit. If there is any chance you will want 2 kWh or a home panel later, starting on an expandable EcoFlow platform avoids paying twice for the same capacity.

mistakes.title: Expecting rated solar wattage from folding panels
mistakes.body: A 200 W panel does not put 200 W into the battery all day. Expect about 60 to 75 percent of rating in good midday sun and four to five peak sun hours, so a 200 W panel realistically adds roughly 480 to 750 Wh on a clear day, less in winter or cloud.

mistakes.title: Leaving the app setup until the outage
mistakes.body: Jackery's fastest wall charging is switched on in its app, and EcoFlow hides charge limits and output modes there too. Install the app, update firmware and set charge limits at home while the power is on, because storms take down both the grid and the cellular data you need.

faqs.a: Neither is better across the board. EcoFlow generally offers more output at each size class, add-on batteries, smart home panels and a deeper app, which makes it stronger for home backup and growing needs. Jackery generally offers lighter units for the capacity, simpler controls and the best single-box 2 kWh option, which suits camping and RV use. Both use LFP batteries on current models and offer roughly five years of warranty coverage.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a Jackery solar generator and a Jackery power station?
faqs.a: Only the bundle. A Jackery solar generator is an Explorer power station sold together with one or more SolarSaga folding panels and the cables to connect them; the station inside is identical to the one sold alone. An EcoFlow solar generator works the same way. Bundles can be good value when discounted, but you can also buy the station alone and add panels later, including third-party panels within its input limits.

faqs.q: Which is better for camping, EcoFlow or Jackery?
faqs.a: For most campers Jackery has the edge at 1 kWh and above because its units are lighter: the Explorer 1000 v2 stores 1,070 Wh at about 24 pounds against about 28 pounds for the Delta 3 Plus, and the Explorer 2000 v2 puts 2 kWh in one 40-pound box. At the small end, EcoFlow's River 3 Plus wins with a 600 W inverter and a snap-on extra battery.

faqs.q: Which is better for home backup during power outages?
faqs.a: EcoFlow is the stronger home-backup platform. The Delta 3 Plus offers 1,800 W, enough for a microwave alongside a fridge, and accepts add-on batteries. The Delta Pro 3 combines 4,096 Wh, 4,000 W and native 120/240 V with a smart home panel and high solar input. Jackery's large Explorer Plus systems also expand, but the ecosystem is narrower. Hardwired circuits need an electrician-installed transfer switch or interlock.

faqs.q: Can I use Jackery solar panels with an EcoFlow power station?
faqs.a: Usually yes, with the right adapter. A panel simply supplies DC power, so what matters is that its voltage and current, alone or wired with others, fall within the station's published solar input range and that the connectors match. Series wiring raises voltage, and cold sunny mornings raise it further, so leave a margin. Add-on batteries and smart panels, by contrast, are brand-specific and never cross over.

faqs.q: How long will an EcoFlow or Jackery power station run a refrigerator?
faqs.a: Use runtime equals watt-hours times 0.85, divided by the average load. A modern fridge uses about 1 to 2 kWh a day, roughly 40 to 85 watts on average. On that basis a Delta 3 Plus or Explorer 1000 v2 runs a typical fridge for about 10 to 20 hours, a 2 kWh unit for roughly a day, and the Delta Pro 3 for about two days.

faqs.q: Are EcoFlow and Jackery power stations expandable?
faqs.a: Most EcoFlow stations are. The River 3 Plus takes a snap-on extra battery, the Delta 3 Plus pairs with extra batteries to reach about 2 kWh and beyond, and the Delta Pro 3 scales into the tens of kilowatt-hours. Jackery's popular Explorer v2 models are fixed-capacity, so the upgrade path is a larger or second unit, although its large Explorer Plus home-backup models do support expansion batteries.

bottomLine:
EcoFlow and Jackery both make good LFP power stations with roughly five-year warranties, so there is no wrong brand here, only the wrong fit. EcoFlow is the better buy when the station lives at home, you want the most output per size class, or you expect to add batteries, a smart panel or a solar array later; the Delta 3 Plus and Delta Pro 3 are its strongest arguments.

Jackery is the better buy when you will carry the station often and already know the size you need; the Explorer 1000 v2 and the single-box Explorer 2000 v2 are the lightest ways to get that capacity. Size your load first with the runtime rule, then let that answer pick the brand.
